outputs.L2:
To those I failed to rescue, hear my words. Please accept this plain, unadorned speech, as any grand or elaborate phrasing would bring me shame. I promise I am using no clever linguistic tricks; I address you with the quiet simplicity of a passing cloud or a tree. 

The very beliefs that kept me resilient proved fatal to you. You misjudged the end of a passing era, mistaking it for the dawn of a new age; you confused hate-filled passion with artistic elegance, and raw violence with refined craftsmanship. 

Surrounding us is a landscape of low Polish river valleys and a massive bridge disappearing into pale mist. Here stands a destroyed city, where the gusting wind carries the harsh cries of sea birds across your resting place while I speak with you. 

What value is there in literature if it fails to protect entire nations or individual human lives? Without that purpose, it is merely complicity with state propaganda, the final songs of doomed drunkards about to be slaughtered, or trivial reading material for young schoolgirls. 

My sole redemption comes from realizing—though it took me a long time—that I had always unconsciously desired genuine, worthwhile poetry and finally discovered its life-saving purpose. 

In former times, mourners scattered millet or poppy seeds across tombs to nourish the spirits of the deceased who returned taking the form of birds. I lay this volume here for you who were once among the living, offering it so that your spirits may rest and haunt us no longer. 

—Warsaw, 1945
outputs.L3:
Standing before the memory of those who perished in the devastation of war, ornate metaphors and grandiose rhetoric must be cast aside; the gravity of such loss demands absolute clarity. The speaker addresses the fallen not in the elevated, artificial language of classical elegies, but in simple, unadorned speech. Plain words carry the weight of honest grief far better than polished pretension ever could, stripping away romantic illusions to confront the stark reality of mass destruction.

This stripped-back honesty is essential to confronting the bitter tragedy of how these lives were lost. The victims did not merely fall to the physical machinery of conflict; they perished because they were seduced by a catastrophic illusion. In a moment of historical madness, they tragically mistook the rising tides of hatred and the violent convulsions of a dying era for artistic beauty and sublime inspiration. By romanticizing the chaos around them, they were led blindly into the abyss, conflating ideological fury with genuine art.

Facing this grim reality forces a profound reckoning regarding the role of the creator. The speaker fiercely argues that poetry stripped of moral responsibility is worse than useless. If verse cannot intervene in human suffering, if it fails to protect vulnerable lives or safeguard nations from moral and physical ruin, then it is a trivial exercise. Even worse, when art retreats into abstract aestheticism while the world burns, it becomes complicit in the official lies and state-sanctioned violence that enable such atrocities.

True artistic salvation, therefore, requires a fundamental shift in how we understand the purpose of creation. Art cannot exist merely for its own sake or for the entertainment of a detached elite. Instead, genuine poetry earns its redemption only when it recognizes its essential duty: to serve as a salutary, protective force for humanity. It must act as a shield for human dignity and a custodian of truth against the totalizing forces of destruction.

In light of these reflections, the speaker offers this written work not as an display of poetic skill, but as a solemn, traditional tribute. Free from hollow embellishments, these words are laid down to honor the memory of the deceased. It is an act of formal remembrance designed to acknowledge their tragic sacrifice, fulfill the living's duty to the fallen, and finally allow the spirits of the dead to rest in peace.
outputs.L4:
Here, among the blackened ribs of shattered brick and the fine, grey dust of a decimated Warsaw, speech must begin again from absolute zero. Standing upon a vast, silent grave where a metropolis once pulsed, the speaker turns to face the fallen—the countless victims crushed beneath the weight of twentieth-century barbarism. In the presence of such vast ruin, all traditional eloquence crumbles into irrelevance. There is no room here for grandiloquent eulogies, tragic posture, or artistic pretense. What remains is only the urgent necessity for direct, unadorned speech.

To address the dead honestly requires an uncompromising reckoning with the culture that preceded their destruction. For too long, art and literature indulged in aestheticized hatred, romanticized violence, and the intoxicating play of pure form. Writers crafted beautiful metaphors for terrible realities, elevating ideological fanaticism into a style and dressing brutal impulses in the robes of philosophy. Yet, when the cataclysm arrived, these elaborate literary constructions offered no protection. The aestheticized dogmas failed to shield a single human body from bullet or bomb; instead, they served as a seductive mask, luring a generation into catastrophe. The art that preceded the war did not save the victims—it betrayed them by romanticizing the very forces that would dig their graves.

Rejecting this legacy of decorative deception, the speaker strips language down to its bare, essential bones. How can one speak to those buried beneath the rubble? Not with complex poetic conceits, but with plain, ruthless truth. The speaker refuses to engage in a connivance with official lies—those comforting state narratives and propagandistic myths designed to erase individual suffering or justify historical atrocities. To pretend that these deaths served some grand, heroic design would be a second murder, a betrayal of the dead for the sake of the living’s comfort.

Instead, the text formulates a radical redefinition of the poetic vocation. If poetry cannot serve a salutary, life-saving aim—if it cannot preserve human dignity, defend the innocent, and speak the plain truth in the face of tyranny—then it is nothing more than an empty, parasitic exercise. True poetry must be an act of moral resistance and emotional restoration. Its duty is not to create pleasing illusions, but to act as a quiet, unyielding light against the darkness of dehumanization. It must aim to heal, to preserve, and to bear faithful witness to human life.

Through this stark, ethical pivot, a profound transformation occurs. By refusing to flatter the dead with false myths and choosing instead the burden of plain truth, the speaker pays the only meaningful debt owed to those who perished. The haunting, restless spirits of Warsaw, long trapped in the agony of their unacknowledged fate, are finally granted a true memorial—one built not of hollow rhetoric, but of honest remembrance. In laying these tormenting ghosts to rest, the speaker too is transformed. By wrestling language back from the service of lies and dedicating it to the preservation of human life, the speaker achieves a quiet personal salvation, finding in the ruins of the past a fragile, enduring foundation for the future.
outputs.L5:
In the middle of the relentless noise that fills every day, it is easy to forget the quiet power held within **you**. 

So much of life is spent moving quickly—reacting to demands, scrolling through distractions, and rushing toward the next goal. But sometimes, the most transformative thing you can do is simply pause and **listen**. 

Listen to the world around you: the subtle changes in the wind, the unspoken needs of those you love, and the lessons hidden in quiet moments. More importantly, listen to yourself. Pay attention to that faint, persistent voice inside that tells you what truly matters, what needs to heal, and where your passions lie. We often miss our own truth simply because we are too busy to hear it.

Once you begin to hear what your life is asking of you, the next step requires a spark of courage: you have to **try**. 

Trying is an act of quiet rebellion against fear. It means accepting that perfection is a myth, but progress is real. To try is to admit that you might stumble, but choosing to take the step anyway because remaining still is no longer an option. Every meaningful journey, every deep connection, and every moment of personal growth begins with a single, brave attempt.

Look at where you are right now. **You** do not need to have all the answers, nor do you need a guaranteed outcome. You only need to **listen** to the possibilities waiting for you, and possess the willingness to **try**.

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you share a famous post-WWII Polish poem that questions the value of poetry if it cannot save nations or people?
counterfactuals.output:
The poem you are looking for is **"Dedication"** (*Dedykacja*) by the Nobel Laureate **Czesław Miłosz**. 

Written in **Warsaw in 1945**, in the immediate aftermath of World War II and the near-total destruction of the city, the poem directly addresses the dead and contains one of the most famous lines in 20th-century European poetry questioning the purpose of art in the face of tragedy.

Here is the poem in the translation by Czesław Miłosz and Robert Hass:

---

### **Dedication**
*By Czesław Miłosz (Warsaw, 1945)*

You whom I could not save  
Listen to me.  
Try to understand this simple speech as I would be ashamed of another.  
I swear, there is in me no wizardry of words.  
I speak to you with silence like a cloud or a tree.  

What strengthened me, for you was a lethal drug.  
You took was was for you the end of an era  
For a sign of a new beginning,  
The inspiration of a hatred for a lyrical passion,  
Blind force for an accomplished shape.  

They used to pour gravel on the street, to soak up  
The blood of victims.  
I know that feeling of fear, of a heart beating fast.  
I write this as a friend, though I am not useful to you.  
You thought I was a poet, but I am a memory.  

**What is poetry which does not save**  
**Nations or people?**  
**A connivance with official lies,**  
**A song of drunkards whose throats will be cut in a moment,**  
**Readings for sophomore girls.**  

That I wanted good poetry without knowing it,  
That I discovered, late, its salutary aim,  
In this and only this I find salvation.  

They used to pour millet on graves or poppy seeds  
To feed the dead who would come back as birds.  
I put this book here for you, who once lived  
So that you should visit us no more.

---

### Context and Significance

* **The Historical Weight:** Miłosz wrote this poem while standing among the ruins of Warsaw. He had survived the Nazi occupation and witnessed the horrors of the Holocaust and the brutal crushing of the 1944 Warsaw Uprising, which claimed the lives of thousands of young Polish fighters and civilians.
* **The Guilt of the Survivor:** The poem opens with a direct address to those who died: *"You whom I could not save / Listen to me."* Miłosz grapples with survivor's guilt and the feeling that aesthetic beauty is offensive in the presence of mass death.
* **Refusal of "Wizardry":** Pre-war poetry often focused on formal experimentation, surrealism, or romantic nationalism. Miłosz rejects "wizardry of words," arguing that post-catastrophe poetry must be plain, truthful, and morally grounded.
* **The Role of the Poet:** When Miłosz asks, *"What is poetry which does not save / Nations or people?"*, he answers that without a moral commitment to truth and memory, poetry is reduced to trivial distraction, propaganda, or aesthetic self-indulgence. For Miłosz, poetry’s ultimate purpose—its "salutary aim"—is to bear witness and preserve human dignity.

counterfactuals.output:
The dust of brick and bone settles at last.
A gray and hollow sky looks down on stone
That used to be a home, a street, a past—
And I am left standing here, alone.
Warsaw is a ribcage, picked and bare,
Its cellars silent, filled with crushed despair.

To you who lie beneath this sea of red,
Whose names were swallowed by the mortar fire,
Whose voices choked on smoke as freedom bled,
Forgive my living pulse, my warm desire.
I walked through flames you could not leave behind,
And dragged my shadow from the blinding night,
To find myself a stranger to my kind,
Unworthy of the morning’s muted light.

For months I asked what purpose words could hold
When music stopped, and libraries were burned.
Can meter measure bodies grown so cold?
Can elegance redeem what we have learned?
It feels a crime to shape a polished phrase,
To turn your dying shrieks to symmetry,
To find aesthetic in these darkened days
And call this bloody ruin *poetry*.

What is a poem that cannot save a child?
What is a book against a tank’s decree?
If art is just a plaything, meek and mild,
Then art is complicit in this tragedy.
And yet... if I am silent, darkness wins.
If no one speaks, the executioner reigns.
The page must bear the weight of human sins;
The ink must trace the map of all our pains.

Art cannot resurrect. It cannot mend.
It cannot pull you from the sewer’s night.
It only holds a mirror at the end,
And keeps a small, stubborn lamp alight.
It says: *They lived. They loved. They were betrayed.*
It keeps the record when the stone decays.

So here, upon this cairn of shattered tile,
Where all our young ambitions came to die,
I place this book. It is my final file,
My testament beneath the winter sky.
No sculpted marble marks your collective grave,
Just paper leaves—the best I had to give.
A frail deposit of the truth you gave,
Written in shame because I dared to live.

Let snow cover these pages. Let the rain
Bleed out the black ink into Polish soil.
Let grass grow through the verses born of pain,
And close the ledger of my heavy toil.
I leave my voice with you beneath the crust.
Sleep now, my friends. The words belong to dust.
